newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - DHL sees Australia warehouse for Asia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - DHL sees Australia warehouse for Asia.

text.p: Global freight giant DHL Worldwide Express is moving fast to complete its new international freight distribution base in Australia aimed at the booming express air cargo markets of Asia.
Using Brisbane airport as the hub, DHL sees its massive "Freight City" concept as challenging Singapore and Hong Kong as the centre of Asian air cargo distribution
"We want to make Australia a warehouse for Asia," DHL's general manager, Brian Roberts told Reuters.
Roberts declined to estimate annual turnover figures for its Australian distribution centre but said it was a "multi-million dollar" operation.
DHL was witnessing a 35 percent annual growth rate for world air cargo into Asia, he said.
"We believe we can double that," Roberts said.

Roberts said DHL's construction of Brisbane airport's Freight City was progressing and expected the first stage, using an initial 5,000 square metres of warehouse and 1,500 square metres of office space, to be completed in February next year.
"There are compelling reasons for this regional warehousing programme to entice multi-nationals from the United States, Europe and Asia," Roberts said.
"Speed, efficiency and a faster time to market are the main factors," he said. "We see it as a long, hard sell with a time frame of 18 months to two years."
Roberts said DHL, in Australia since 1974, targeted Brisbane Airport because of cost-competitiveness and its ideal physical location for entry into Asia.

The group had the backing of the Federal Airports Authority (FAC), the Queensland State government and was in talks with the Federal Government over a plan for the site to become an international economic development zone, Roberts said.
"This is a window of opportunity. If we don't put ourselves on the map here, we won't have their (the Multinationals) confidence," he said.
"I also believe we will never get a manufacturing industry here (in Australia) if we're not supplying the whole Asian market," Roberts said.
The attraction for DHL was the ability to link with aircraft to its Manila hub, thus offering a 24-hour overnight service to Asia.
The FAC said current international cargo throughput for Brisbane airport was more than 75,000 tonnes a year and had been growing at a compound rate of 13 percent over the last decade.
The Freight City concept, using 41 hectares, had the capacity to handle over one million tonnes of cargo annually when fully developed, the FAC said.

In a submission to an Australian parliamentary air freight review inquiry this year, DHL said alongside cost savings, Australia could provide the same transit time to Asia as that from Hong Kong or Singapore.
"Australia is also the second-largest distributor centre for high-tech and value-added products after Japan," Roberts said.
"Japan is far too expensive," he said. "Our vision is to have (the Brisbane complex) as a state-of-the-art handling, storage and distribution facility," Roberts said.
DHL saw its new Australian overnight delivery pipeline in the same league as its Brussels home base and similar DHL centres in Bahrain and Cincinatti, he said.

While moving its new customer service centre to Brisbane from Sydney, DHL also planned to expand into Melbourne and Perth airports, offering warehousing, pick-and-pack and inventory control services, Roberts said.
The main shareholders in DHL are Deutsche Lufthansa AG and Japan Airlines Co Ltd, which each hold a 25 percent stake.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
